utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I understand, Ms. Somers --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- summary to us over the phone. In the course of that, it became eminently clear that materials were being addressed that had not been raised either in the initial proofing, or in the initial summaries, and also there are, in our view, clear 90(H) violations as to Admiral Jokic's testimony. I've asked Mr. Re to please prepare an ore tenus application on what we are asking the Chamber to do about this situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution has an application that we move an oral motion to exclude evidence, the anticipated evidence of this particular witness, Mr. Jovanovic, evidence which goes outside the summaries provided earlier to the Office of the Prosecutor. I can briefly outline to Your Honours the history of this and why we're making this application, and why we're doing it - it's 10 past 9.00 - this morning in the absence of the witness. When the Defence filed their summaries pursuant to Rule 65 ter on the 25th of June, 2004 the -- it's paragraph 15. The Prosecution was informed that this particular witness, who was the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Partisan Motorised Brigade was going to testify as to the following points: One, how he took over the command of his unit, the positions of -- two, the position of units under his command; three, the command on communication issues within the 9th VPS in the period in which he acted as the commander of the 3rd Battalion; the next one is during the 6th of December, he was the direct participant of the events that took place on the said date. He will testify on fire his units opened on Croatian forces on that day. He will testify on activities of Croatian forces from Dubrovnik on that day. He will testify how he was removed from duty on that day and how he reported to the command of the VPS on the events of the 6th of December. As Your Honour, Presiding Judge, Judge Parker, rightly said in your observations on the Status Conference before the Defence case started, the summaries were fairly vague. Now, this is a fairly vague summary. But within that it is a workable summary as to what the Prosecution is to expect. It's not a summary of the facts as the Rules mandate but it's a working summary of the areas in which you might expect that the witness may testify. And this was the basis upon which the Prosecution was preparing to cross-examine this particular witness. The Defence counsel promised us additional -- after Your Honour ordered Defence counsel before the start of the Defence case to provide better summaries before the witness testified. We were promised a "better summary" and last night the Prosecution -- I withdraw that. Earlier this week, the Prosecution received a document from the Defence. It was on the 11th of January -- 11th of July, dated -- we received it on the 11th of July, and it is a report which the witness wrote apparently on the 6th of the December, outlining the activities of the -- outlining what he said occurred on that particular day. The Defence will, I anticipate, tender this document and the Prosecution of course has no objection to it. The relevant portion of this is that the witness in that report, which was dated on the 6th of December, 1991 and is a contemporaneous document, a handwritten document, apparently prepared on that day, said, at paragraph 2 -- paragraph 1: "On the 6th of December, 1991, at around 6.00, the command location at a Osojnik I received a request by means of communication from the commander of the 3rd of the 472nd Kovacevic to support him with mortar activity in Lazaret. Paragraph 2: As Captain Kovacevic had presented the plan of the carrying out of the combat activities precisely during the previous day, I had understood that the same was approved by the commander of the 9th VPS, and thus I immediately went and manned the observation post in the region of Laski Brijeg. So those are the two pieces of evidence that we were advised of. That Kovacevic had ordered the attack, this witness had apparently been presented with this plan the day before, and because -- and he had understood that it must have been approved by the commander of the VPS, namely, I imagine, Admiral Jokic. While awaiting for further summary, we received a telephone call last night. We were still waiting here for this information after 10.00 last night. And Mr. Rodic's legal assistant dictated to us for the next half an hour these vital missing additional pieces of evidence with which he intends to call from this witness this morning. And this piece of evidence appears in a summary which we received upon arriving at work after leaving at 11.30 last night and coming in this morning, we found a written version of this, a written version of what was told to us on the phone. And that is that on the 5th of December, the witness went to a briefing at the command post in Kupari and Admiral Jokic was indeed present there. And at that briefing, Captain Kovacevic presented a plan to overcome the "Srdj problem" and the problem of constant provocations and recommended a plan of how to solve the Srdj problem, saying that he could solve the problem easily and expeditiously. The plan of the attack on Srdj envisaged the cooperation and support of the 3rd and the 5th as well as the cannon battery of the 130-millimetre from Cilipi. The witness asked the commander of the 9th VPS, Admiral Jokic, when the realisation of the cooperation task should begin. The admiral responded that he, the witness, would be informed. After the event the witness left the briefing. "In the next day," the commander - that's Kovacevic - "requested his assistance, and the witness opened fire on two occasions." Now, the difficulty with this is this is the first time this piece of information as to Admiral Jokic's alleged involvement in ordering the attack on Srdj has surfaced in the entire trial. That is the first piece of direct evidence in relation to Admiral Jokic approving, condoning, or ordering the attack on Srdj the next morning, after we've heard a great deal of evidence about his participation in trying to arrange a cease-fire that very same day. This information was not in the Defence pre-trial brief filed in December last year. This vital piece of information was not in the Defence opening statement made a mere two weeks ago. It was not in the Defence summary provided to us in the last week of June. And it's a flagrant violation of Rule 90(H) because it was never put to Admiral Jokic at any point in his lengthy cross-examination. And this piece of information in the Prosecution's submission cannot have been a secret. It cannot only have emerged at 10.00 last night, presumably when Mr. Petrovic had been speaking to the witness somewhere else in proofing him. The Prosecution is unable to meet this piece of information at this late stage. Receiving this information just before 11.00 last night, we are simply unable to prepare for a proper cross-examination, find the relevant transcript references, find the relevant documents, and adequately represent the Prosecution's interests in putting the case to this witness. And of course, there's another difficulty in relation to this, which comes directly from the failure of the Defence to put this apparently now vital part of their changing defence to Admiral Jokic in his cross-examination, and that is, we have not had a chance and will not have a chance to speak to Admiral Jokic to find out the veracity of this information. We cannot check with Jokic, so we do not have a good faith basis on which we can cross-examine this witness as to whether or not this in fact occurred. The only hint, so to speak, that something like this may be coming was in briefing notes we received on Sunday night - when of course we weren't here - at 7.30 on Sunday night, receiving them on Monday morning, in relation to the evidence of the witness Stojanovic. Now, Mr. Stojanovic's evidence was of his hearing from Kovacevic that he had attended a briefing at which Admiral Jokic had been present. But the way it was presented was hearsay evidence, and of course the Prosecution had no good-faith basis upon which we could challenge the witness as to whether or not Kovacevic had said it, as opposed to whether or not the meeting or the briefing at Kupari had in fact occurred. Because the Prosecution clearly hasn't spoken to Kovacevic, and we are not in a position to challenge the witness as to whether or not Kovacevic said it, as opposed to whether or not the meeting actually occurred. There is a further piece of evidence in -- a further piece in this summary which is also provided in writing this morning and notified to us between 10.30 and 11.00 last night, and that goes to the method and means of this witness's removal from his post on the 6th of December. And this is: During the afternoon hours, the witness, again in response to Croat targets that were fired again in response to the Croat targets that were firing at his unit. "At 1800 hours, Colonel Kovacevic, Gavro, came to the unit, his unit, and transmitted the order of Admiral Jokic that pursuant to the order of General Kadijevic, he must immediately leave his duty, of which his brigade was informed." Again, this missing piece of information that it was in fact General Kadijevic who ordered Jokic to relieve this person -- relieve Mr. Jovanovic of his command was not put to Admiral Jokic, was not in the summaries, and, as far as the Prosecution can tell, in the time in which we have been given to research this issue, has newly arisen in the trial. The Prosecution, of course, appreciate -- we of course appreciate our greater resources, but the principle of equality of arms applies equally to both sides in the conduct of proceedings before this Tribunal. The purpose of summaries is to ensure that both sides are on notice of the facts - the facts, not the evidence, the facts - which are to be led to give them time to prepare the case, so that the case can be properly presented, and the Trial Chamber has the basis upon which it can properly determine the matter. Now, the Prosecution's application is that the evidence in relation to Admiral Jokic's alleged attendance in this meeting and his alleged condoning be excluded today, because the Prosecution is simply not in a position to make the appropriate inquiries of Admiral Jokic to be in a position to cross-examine the witness. And we also make the application in relation to the extra piece of evidence about General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There has been discussion already earlier on -- I'm sorry. I apologise. The interpretation was not proper. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It has now come through in English. Thank you. Have you got yours, Mr. Rodic? Yes, it appears to be in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Now I can hear. It is true, Your Honour, that in the past couple of days, there has been discussion about the summaries, and my learned colleagues had protested either to them lacking information or not having been given on time. However, I have to point out, without going again into the situation the Defence finds itself in, that we have managed to come into contact with some of our witnesses only in the break between the end of the Prosecution case and the start of the Defence case. Concerning this particular witness, the case is again the same. What is typical of this particular witness, as you see, is also that his inability to come and appear before the Honourable Trial Chamber because of a number of problems of a private nature that he experiences and because there is also involved a certain fear concerning some of the allegations contained in the charges. In the summary which was delivered to our learned colleagues under the 65 ter Rule, my learned colleague was -- did quote correctly what was contained therein. However, I have to say that at a later date, the Defence received a document which was a report on the combat activities of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Partisan Motorised Brigade, drafted on the 6th of December, 1991, which was authored by this particular witness. When we confronted the witness with this particular document, we obtained some new data, as presented to you now by my learned colleague. In a part of what he said, something has been left out, which was -- it was only item 2 of this particular report that my learned colleague read to you, and it says: "As the concept of the combat activities had been specifically presented by Captain Kovacevic the day before," this is what the sentence read, basically. I believe it was here read differently. And in the proofing, which again had some technical difficulties, we contacted our learned colleagues from the OTP around 9.00 last night, but then we had some technical difficulties, and in order to do it -- to deliver the information as soon as possible, we decided to do it over the phone. It was only late last night when our equipment started working again. We also sent the written summary of what had been dictated over the phone earlier on. And this is the result of the proofing that my colleague, Vladimir Petrovic, carried out while talking to this witness in Belgrade. As for this crucial sentence that was pointed out to by my learned colleague, and that is that Captain Kovacevic had specifically presented the concept of the combat activities, and as I understood, it had been approved by the command of the 9th VPS, and I immediately headed out to the observation point in Laski Brijeg in order to directly coordinate the action. In the proofing summary that the OTP had been informed of, there are also words of the witness to the effect that he had asked Admiral Jokic as to when the task would be realised and that the admiral had replied to him, "You will be informed of it." Therefore, these are the two issues which my learned colleague Re has left out now in presenting this matter to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Rodic. We'd heard both of those matters during Mr. Re's submission. I recall both of them. So he didn't leave them out. But anyhow, move on to your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I certainly didn't hear Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the second reference in my headphones. I didn't hear it in interpretation. However, even earlier, my colleagues from the Prosecution objected that certain things had not been put to Admiral Jokic. Simply speaking, we were unable to put everything to Admiral Jokic, what was available to the Defence at that moment, be it in the form of document or a brief or proofing notes or investigator's notes, was put to the witness and attempt has been made to go through it in the course of cross-examination. So far in presenting our defence case, witnesses have appeared, such as company commanders, and a commander of the 130-millimetre battery, whose testimony clearly pointed to the attack on Srdj on the 6th of December, 1991, specifying that this attack originated from the command of the 9th VPS. Compared to all those witnesses, this one is the only one whose position enabled him at the time to attend personally the briefings held at the command of the 9th VPS at the forward command post in Kupari. This report -- Your Honours, we have another technical problem with interpretation. French seems to be heard on the B/C/S channel. Let me continue. This report referenced by my learned friend Re of the 6th of December was submitted to the Prosecution last Friday, as I say, last Friday. And this report contains a number of other elements that I cannot read now, but which precisely point to the subject matter of the testimony of previous witnesses called by the Defence. In those terms, the report submitted seven days ago is not different from the summary, and I believe it was sufficient in order to be put to Admiral Jokic, to be clarified with him in cross-examination if my learned friends deemed that necessary when he testified about his agreement. The discrepancy between the arguments between this report and his testimony are eminently clear. I'm just explaining how this came about. Last night at 10.00 p.m., we succeeded in dictating over the telephone the proofing summary we received from Belgrade. However, this report was submitted last Friday, and it is very clear in speaking to this whole operation on Srdj and the attack of the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, first, what is apparent from all you say, that you're putting all of this on the basis that for the first time, this witness has been briefed, proofed, to give evidence. Clearly, this problem arises because there has not been an adequate proofing of the witness in the preparation of the Defence case at the proper time. You're saying now that most material information only came to your notice during yesterday's proofing. If the witness had been adequately proofed for the purposes of the 65 ter and for the purpose of the preparation of your case, the materiality of these two disputed issues would have been starkly obvious. The second comment that I have is that we have -- well, I'll leave it for the moment and ask you about the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have already tried to explain that concerning the issue of detecting witnesses and concerning the issue of their goodwill and willingness to talk on this subject, the Defence faced genuinely enormous problems. Things started to unfold, if I may say so, only later, and specifically in relation to this witness, I tried to explain, that was because he had a number of problems of a private nature, related to his participation in this operation on Srdj. I don't know if he's listening to this, and I can understand his misgivings, but he was less than eager to talk. In the process of collecting other information, as that other information came in, we approached the witness again in order to try to elucidate and clarify the events. The third stage in that process is the subsequent emergence of this report, which had been requested a long time ago, even before the trial began. However, the Defence had no access to it. The Defence didn't even know whether it was still in existence or had been destroyed. We only now managed to lay our hands on it. And from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When did you first see this report, and from what source did you obtain it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this report comes from the military archives. It had been requested from three different places: From the navy, from the operations group, and from the archives in Belgrade. We located the report just before leaving for The Hague. On the eve of our Defence case, and it was in the course of presenting our case we received the report according to all the rules and regulations, and we succeeded precisely because of the importance of this document in getting it physically, although that too had been a huge problem. I believe, Your Honour, and I'm sorry if I'm interrupting you, but I have to say, if I'm talking about this: You have heard references in the course of examining Vlado Sikimic, operations officer at the forward command post, to the war journal of the 9th VPS in Kupari that was introduced through that witness. And the question of the war journal arose, the war journal from the basic command post at Kupari, which Petre Handzijev, another witness, also talked about. We did not locate this document. That document -- in fact, this report, just as the war journal from the forward command post in Kupari, fall within the same category of documents, which must be archived permanently. However, we still have not located it. In keeping with our Defence case and all that we presented before this Trial Chamber, we shall continue in our efforts to find it, until the end of our case, because it is very important for us to find out whether the document has been destroyed or, alternatively, to get it, because it can be very important in corroborating and further clarifying everything that was said by Defence witnesses. Furthermore, Admiral Jokic mentioned a report made by Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have me a little confused, Mr. Rodic. I understood that you now have the report of the witness which he prepared on the 6th of December. Is that the report you're just saying that you're still trying to locate? Or is it a different report?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. This report of the 6th of December, written by witness Jovanovic, we succeeded in securing and providing during the Defence case, according to all the Rules. I'm now talking about the report that Admiral Jokic said was written by Captain Kovacevic, commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade at that time, and I'm saying that this is very important because it was also written on the 6th of December. We did an enormous work trying to locate it, but we have not succeeded yet, and that one is certainly also very important to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You haven't yet said where it was that you found the report of this witness written on the 6th of December. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to be specific, we found it in Kumbor. It was located in Kumbor, at the command of the navy. And we were first informed of this report by the current Chief of Staff of the navy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was late in June, seven or eight days before the beginning of the Defence case. I cannot remember the exact date, but I know it was very shortly before the beginning of the Defence case, before our journey. That document, therefore, was located, but without an official approval of the official authorities, without their confirmation that it had been duly registered and without their certification that it is an original document. We were unable to get it. We did get that certification later, in Belgrade, and instigated -- or rather, instituted proceedings to be issued with that document. And as I said, we received it already in the course of presenting our Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, were you wanting to put further matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I believe I responded to your question. If my answer has been sufficient. You asked me to reply to your first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've managed to cover the second in the course of dealing with the first, so that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn for a few moments to consider this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the Chamber adjourns, may I just bring up one point that I think I would like to refresh the Chamber's recollection, although I'm sure you recall. The basis for videolink was that the defendant -- I'm sorry, the accused -- the witness is prevented from physically appearing before the Trial Chamber due to several factors that pose as a serious impediment, namely, the person is a former military officer and presently a pensioner, is of a considerable age and fragile health, and as such travel is a risk and onerous undertaking which he would rather avoid. Then: The wife of the individual is seriously ill and under constant medical supervision. As a result, the individual refuses to leave the country as long as his spouse is ill and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will repeat it. As a result, the witness refuses to leave the country as long as his spouse is ill and frail. The Defence is of the opinion that the witness's position on the matter is quite understandable, since it is rather difficult to ask of a person to embark on such a peculiar journey while his loved one is seriously ill. I simply bring to the Chamber's attention that at no time was there any mention of fear of role or legal implications or potential criminal culpability, and for such matters, if in fact that is a concern, and it appears that somewhere it may be at a higher point on the list than the other factors, of course, safe conduct is an option. But the Prosecution expressed its opinion on it, as was requested by the Chamber, based on what we had represented to us in the submission. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now adjourn for a short time. --- Break taken at 9.48 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are objections to two pieces of evidence that it appears intended to lead from the witness to be called this morning. The first concerns a briefing at the command post at Kupari on the evening of the 5th of December, in which the witness will say he was a participant, at which meeting he will indicate there was present also the earlier Prosecution witness, Admiral Jokic, who was present throughout the briefing and who directly responded to the witness by telling him he would be informed when the briefing was to be implemented. There can be no question of the materiality, somewhat critical materiality, of that piece of evidence in the context of the facts of this case. It was not the subject of a pre-trial disclosure. It was not put to Admiral Jokic. It clearly was a matter which, if then known to the Defence, should have been put to Admiral Jokic, pursuant to Rule 90(H) of the Rules. That was not done. The second objection is to evidence concerning the circumstances in which the witness came to be relieved of his command of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade on the evening of the 6th of December. The critical point of the concern is evidence that it was said by the colonel who was relieving the witness of his command that he was acting on the order of General Kadijevic in doing so. This is a matter which comes within the scope of the general notice of evidence given in respect of this matter, that is, the circumstances in which he came to be relieved of his command, but it is clearly a matter which was contrary to the evidence of Admiral Jokic given in the course of the Prosecution case. So, then known to the Defence, it ought to have been put to the admiral in cross-examination. It is said in respect of both pieces of information that they have come to the knowledge of the Defence, in effect, yesterday, and notice of each matter, it is accepted, was given late last evening. The witness is not a surprise witness. It is a witness that has been planned to be called by the Defence. What is offered by way of explanation is that the Defence were not aware that the witness would say each of these things. A report came to their possession from official records at Kumbor a little under a week before the Defence team returned to The Hague to commence the Defence case. That report does not specifically disclose the first matter, from what we have been told, but it does the second. Of course, Admiral Jokic gave his evidence some months ago, and if this matter was not to the knowledge of the Defence at that time, there is an explanation for the failure to put each of these matters to the admiral. The explanation offered suggests that the report, insofar as it might have disclosed the second matter, was not in the possession of the Defence when they complied with 65 ter. And the report itself does not disclose the first. It is apparent that what happened yesterday is that Mr. Petrovic proofed the witness in some detail, and each of these matters and their relevance to the Defence case became obvious, and therefore, late in the evening, notice was given to the Prosecution. If it be accepted that the Defence first knew of the report and its indication of the second matter only something a little short of a week before coming again to The Hague to commence the Defence case, one can understand that there may have not been earlier notice of that matter. What is apparent, however, is that in both matters there has been a failure by the Defence to properly proof this witness at and before the commencement of the trial. There is no suggestion that the witness was unknown to the Defence; in fact, his relevance and role is obvious. While it is said that he may have had some reluctance to speak to the Defence, what is put before us on official applications does not suggest that he was not prepared to speak, and it is clear that when it was approached on the eve of actually giving evidence, these matters were disclosed by the witness. In short, there has been a failure to do what should have been done on the part of the Defence in the proofing of this witness, and it has had an adverse effect on the proper conduct of the trial. The question is: What, in the circumstances, should the Trial Chamber do about this, having to be guided in the end by the interests of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. justice? There has been at least a failure to comply with the requirements of Rule 90(H), due to a failure to adequately proof the witness. But, of course, it does not automatically or necessarily follow from that that the evidence should be excluded. Both pieces of evidence are, as I have indicated, clearly material, if that proves to be the evidence given by the witness. The Chamber, in the end, is of the view that, despite the way in which this has occurred, due to neglect, the interests of justice require, on balance, that this evidence be allowed to be led. Clearly, when we come to weigh the evidence, the failure to deal with it in the proper way in the course of trial may well come to have a significance to the Chamber as it comes to assess its weight. It is too early yet to have any concluded view about that. We have yet to see and hear the witness. But the way in which the matter has been improperly managed will well possibly have a bearing upon the weight that we can attach to one or other or both of these matters of evidence. Clearly, both of these matters ought to have been put to Admiral Jokic, at least. The Chamber's view that both pieces of evidence should be allowed to be led, if it is indeed is the evidence of the witness, inevitably leads the Chamber to the view that if the Prosecution so wishes, they should be allowed to recall the admiral on these two issues, if they so wish. They may well want to lead other evidence relative to these facts. If so, an application would need to be made. We appreciate the Prosecution concern that they are in some embarrassment because of the incredibly short notice that they have had of these two material pieces of evidence. They will, as they have on other occasions, no doubt do what they can with this. If there seems to be some impossibility, that will need to be specifically raised with the Chamber. So the ruling of the Chamber is that the Prosecution motion for the non-reception of each of these pieces of evidence will not be granted. The evidence may be led, if that is how it comes, and there is leave to the Prosecution to recall in rebuttal Admiral Jokic, should the Prosecution be so minded. And if there are other issues that arise, the Chamber will obviously be prepared to hear those matters on their merit. Now, we have spent the first hour and a half of today on this issue. There is a videolink, and we really need to get on with it. Is there any difficulty seen in proceeding with that immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just have one very minor matter arising from Your Honour's ruling, that is, in your ruling, Your Honours referred to the second matter, that is, the manner of the witness's removal by -- on the order apparently of General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The mention of General Kadijevic as the source of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's the point of the second objection, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour in your ruling said that it appeared in the report of the 6th of December whereas the first one didn't. That is in fact not so. And if somehow in the exchange it may have got lost, neither appeared in the report of the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The Chamber doesn't have the report, of course. We had -- or at least I had, I believe the other Judges too, had had the impression that that was flagged in the report. It makes, I'm afraid, no difference to the decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only thing I say in relation to the ruling from the Prosecution's viewpoint is that the Prosecution does not believe it could be in a position to cross-examine the witness on the point without first speaking to Admiral Jokic, because I just don't see I have a basis upon which I can challenge it. Because it will be sworn evidence before the -- before the Trial Chamber, and I may have to request an adjournment of the cross-examination on the particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wish it was as easy as that. You may have to, and we may well have to accede to it. But the problem is re-establishing a videolink at some later time at short notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. On that point, if I may. If it turns out that the basis for the videolink in fact may not have been exactly as suggested, perhaps the witness could be considered to come in live, given what has come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you know how long it takes to get the necessary visas, et cetera, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I am aware, Your Honour. But perhaps the Defence is on notice that if they might want to consider, if the Chamber is so minded, to beginning that process, should the need arise. And they have their representative presently there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will cross that bridge if and when it should be reached. We will proceed now to connect to the videolink and commence the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Good morning, Your Honour. I will get the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Do you have there the affirmation card?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] It's on the screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Would you please read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Miroslav Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, may I please ask you, right at the outset, for proceedings to go smoothly and in order that we may record everything that you say, can you please make a brief pause between question and answer, a brief pause, please. And also, please provide brief answers to the questions I ask you. Thank you. Mr. Jovanovic, when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of October, 1946, in Prokuplje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was retired, with the rank of colonel, on the 3rd of July, 1998, retired from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were military schools, the military academy for land forces in 1968 and the command staff academy in 1982.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you start serving in the army?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I started serving with the JNA on the 1st of September, 1968.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, throughout your military career, where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I spent most of my time in Titograd, nowadays called Podgorica, in the garrisons of Kolasin, Bar and Podgorica, and I spent some time in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, can you please tell us which unit you were part of in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 5th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was the brigade's Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend a long time in that post?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you held that post, did the brigade commanders change?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many commanders came and went?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the brigade command, a total of three brigade commanders changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what your rank was at the time when you were Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Establishment-wise, the 5th Brigade, it was part of which larger unit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was within the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, throughout 1991, were any units detached from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which specific unit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Within the 9th Naval Sector, it was the 3rd Battalion that was attached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the 3rd Battalion of your brigade was detached from its original composition and attached to the 9th VPS; is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade was re-subordinated to the command of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In early October 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 3rd Battalion was attached to the 9th VPS, where did the battalion stay, around October?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion was carrying out tasks within the VPS, along the Herceg-Novi, Debeli Brijeg, Kupari axis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this battalion take part in the land blockade of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the axis of the blockade along which the positions of the 3rd Battalion were?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion, during the blockade of Dubrovnik, stayed in the area of Zaton, the area of Petrovo Selo and Osojnak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Osojnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P124. It's a map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Can you please put the map on the ELMO. I was not given a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, can you see the map?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't read the caption, but I see which area is depicted on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the registrar please tell us whether they have the map, if you don't have P124.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] I was not given P124.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the map marked as P132?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] I have no map. However, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should now be visible on the screen. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at this map, can you see the positions of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade on it? Can you see the positions on the map?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise the area where the battalion was deployed, but I can't see the names of the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. It must be a technical problem we're facing. Let's move on, please. We'll no longer be needing this map. Mr. Jovanovic, throughout October, November, and December 1991, did the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade stay throughout this time in the Dubrovnik and Herzegovina theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The battalion was -- throughout this time within the composition of the 9th VPS, except for late October and early November, when it had been pulled out from the area of war operations and sent to the Podgorica area, so that they could rest and receive reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade, when did it return to the Dubrovnik, Herzegovina theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In early November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which specific tasks did it take part in, in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The blockade of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the command of the 5th Brigade. I worked as the brigade's Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early December 1991, where was the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade positioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion was carrying out tasks related to the blockade of Dubrovnik. It was at the positions of Zaton, Petrovo Selo, and Osojnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout this period of time, October through December 1991, did you at any point in time take over command over the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how that came about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Men needed to rest, and the battalion commander Zdravkovic had to deal with some family problems that he had at the time. Therefore, the command of the 9th VPS sent a request to the brigade command to send over an officer from their own ranks who could successfully exercise command over the battalion while the battalion commander Zdravkovic was absent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how you took over command of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to orders from the brigade commander, I had received a transfer to the battalion, and command was handed over to me by Major Zdravkovic. I familiarised myself with the situation, area of deployment, and the tasks faced by the battalion. And we informed the command of the 9th VPS about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the existence of the 2nd Operations Group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While carrying out your duties and tasks, did you have any contact with the 2nd Operations Group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, can you please explain how the communications lines in your battalion worked. What sort of equipment did you have? What communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Our communication lines worked fine, because practically the only thing we used were the wire links between the command of the VPS and the battalion, and also between the battalion command and its subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you said that you had a communication line open to the command of the VPS and also to the commanders of the subordinated units that were under your battalion.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what was the discipline like in the unit that you took over in early December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were men with some war experience. They had been tried and true, and they had been perfectly trained. They were extremely disciplined. The tasks were clear and were carried out impeccably, those tasks that they had been assigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was control and command like in the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion commander commanded the battalion. As for day-to-day activities, we had daily briefings or reports to the command of the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend briefings or reports at the command of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did those briefings at the command of the 9th VPS take place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The briefings took place at the command post of the 9th VPS in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who chaired these briefings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 9th VPS did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 9th VPS at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Vice Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, can you tell us who else was present at these briefings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The briefings were attended by commanders of subordinate units, the VPS Chief of Staff, warship Captain Milan Zec; and bodies that were within the command of the military naval sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time roughly were these briefings held?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The briefings, for the most part, were held in the evening, usually gone 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, did you attend the briefing at the forward command post in Kupari on the 5th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who chaired that particular briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Commander Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were those present?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Commanders of subordinate units, Chief of Staff, warship Captain Milan Zec, and bodies of the command of the military naval sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Vladimir Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which position did he hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. He was directly subordinated to Commander Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This briefing on the 5th of December, 1991, was it attended by Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Kovacevic address those at the briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us what he talked about.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He talked about the problems that he was experiencing in the Srdj area, where he was constantly exposed to provocations from the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was exposed to a daily gunfire, and his forces were constantly under fire. He suggested that he should solve this problem by seizing Srdj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Kovacevic say how he was going to achieve this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us in some detail what it was that he said to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He asked that he be permitted to use his assault units and the units present on the front line with artillery support, in order to carry out an attack and seize Srdj. He was adamant that he was going to be able to achieve this action in a very fast manner and a very efficient manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His proposal for the attack on Srdj, what did it include in terms of coordination and support?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The proposal envisaged the support of 130-millimetre Howitzers and of the fire group of -- the firing group of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This unit that had the artillery pieces of 130-millimetre calibre, do you know where it was positioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that it was somewhere in the Cilipi area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Chief of Staff of the 9th VPS, warship Captain Milan Zec, take part in this briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything with regard to this proposal put forward by Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what it was that the Chief of Staff said.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He pointed out that if the action were to be allowed, the action on Srdj, that it had to be finished by 1200 hours on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, did you raise any questions at this briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon the end of the briefing, before leaving the command post of the 9th VPS, I asked Commander Jokic as to whether the action was going to be allowed, approved. And since I did not get any answer, I asked to be timely informed of the time of the commencement of the action, in order for me to be able to undertake all the planned actions geared toward the implementation of the action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the commander answer this question of yours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any indication given to you as to how you were about to be notified? Did anyone tell you anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually. And it would have been normal for them to inform me about it over the usual communications things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there until the very end of the briefing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know when the action was supposed to start?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was this going to be dealt with? How would you find out?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to be informed by the command of the 9th VPS or by Commander Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there at the forward command post at Kupari, from those who were present there, did you hear anything about the action not being approved, not being planned to be carried out, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Kovacevic leave the room where the briefing took place together with you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He remained seated in his place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else stay on with him after you left the place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The entire VPS command remained there, together with Admiral Jokic and some of the commanders who had taken part in the briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jovanovic: Where were you headed? Where did you go when you left the briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I headed for my command post in the Osojnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was going on on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning hours, somewhere between 6.00 and 7.00 in the morning, Captain Kovacevic informed me that he was under heavy fire from the Croatian forces and that he was asking for the support of 130-millimetre Howitzers and of the fire support group of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he request fire support from your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction? What did you do upon receiving the request?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon receiving the request, I headed to my observation point, observation post, where I ordered that positions be taken and organised the support, opening fire on the targets that were distinguished as the points from where the fire was coming, in the Lazaret area and Nuncijata.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, when you were on the observation post, what did you observe? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the observation post, both I and my associates there clearly saw the fire coming from mortars of the Croatian forces from the area of Lazaret and Nuncijata.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jovanovic: Where were the weapons that you intended to use?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The fire support weapons of the 3rd Battalion were deployed on the firing positions south of Osojnik, so that you can see Vis to the south of Osojnik, the elevation point was 443 or 442.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which fire support weapons did you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the battalion, we had 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me -- I apologise. I've interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Recoilless guns, hand-held rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ultimate range of -- maximum range of 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: 120-millimetre mortars can effectively fire to a distance of up to six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall which points in the direction of the town of Dubrovnik constitute the maximum range to be reached by your weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to visualise now the situation as we saw it on the map, which is the northern slope of Babin Kuk, which is Velika Petka. That is closer to us, meaning us from -- watching from Osojnik. And to the east, the slopes of Srdj, that is, Nuncijata, Sustjepan, the left bank of Dubravacka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, did you notice the firing positions of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was fire being opened from these enemy firing positions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fire upon these -- the seen distinguished firing positions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: After having opened fire, did you notify anyone thereof?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who it was that you notified.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I informed the operations centre of the 9th VPS about the cause of the action and about the fire support being provided, the weapons involved, and the targets involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the operations centre of the 9th VPS, can you tell us, for the sake of precision, where this operations centre was located.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The operations centre of the 9th VPS was at the forward command post in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The action that you've described to us now, was that the only request issued by Captain Kovacevic on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another request?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Captain Kovacevic requested that second time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Kovacevic asked for urgent support to be directed at Lazaret, Nuncijata, and Hotel Libertas, and he particularly mentioned the importance of using 130-millimetre Howitzers as fire support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform the operations centre of the 9th VPS about this particular request by Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you follow up with an action based on that request?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my area of responsibility, that is, firing at the targets within range of my weapons, that is, Lazareti, Nuncijata, without knowing whether actually the 9th VPS got the request for the fire support for Hotel Libertas. This was something I was not directly involved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Kovacevic perhaps mention why it was that he requested the 130-millimetre artillery support?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He said that he was under heavy fire coming from the area of Hotel Libertas and that he had sustained great casualties in the Srdj area, that he was not able to fire upon these positions, and that to his estimate, only 130-millimetre Howitzers were able to carry out the action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jovanovic: Do you remember the time of this second action of yours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would refer you to my report, because it was on the basis of the notes I made that I drafted the report. It was after 9.00. It was approximately 9.15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you received this second request by Captain Kovacevic, asking your support and the support of 130-millimetre artillery, did you inform the operations centre of the 9th VPS thereof?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember up until what time you were opening fire from your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until 11.45.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do then, Mr. Jovanovic, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I informed the operations centre of the 9th VPS about the fact that we were providing support and asked of them whether we should continue providing our support to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you guided by when you asked the question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: By the order of the warship Captain Milan Zec of the day before, of the evening before, which stated that the activities around the Srdj area had to be terminated by 1200 hours, when a complete, total peace should set in, should be secured. And I'm here quoting exactly what warship Captain Milan Zec said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those at the operations centre of the 9th VPS, what did they tell you when you asked them at 11.55 what it was that you should do next?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The duty-officer at the operations centre conveyed to me the order of the commander of the 9th VPS that the order concerning the total peace should be fully honoured and that any ongoing activities should be terminated, as well as that I should report to the operations centre and brief them about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, the order that you received from the operations centre at 11.55, of the operations centre of the 9th VPS, concerning the termination of all activities, prior to that, were you banned by anyone or prevented from using your weapons, by anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then indeed report to the forward command post at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Who did you find at the forward command post at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I found a duty-officer there, Lieutenant Colonel Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Lieutenant Colonel Kozaric tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Kozaric transmitted to me the order of the sector commander to write a report, and he also said that the sector commander had been invited to see the federal secretary, the report, urgently, and that it was probable that the entire command of the 9th VPS would be replaced as a result of the firing action upon the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the federal secretary at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, did you indeed write that report?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was keeping my war journal, my own notebook, at the observation post, I took that material, and referring to the notebook the times and various entries, I wrote the report and left it with the duty operations officer at the command of the VPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the usher's assistance, I would like to have one document distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I have just handed out a document, and so that you are informed, it is a report on the combat activities of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade, submitted to the command of the 9th VPS on the 6th of December, 1991. Do you have that document before you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, do you recognise this document? Can you tell us, is that your report?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We need it on the ELMO if it is going to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The document before me is my own report. However, I see a different report on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you the version of that document in the Serbo-Croat language?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read to us the heading on that document.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Command of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Infantry Motorised Brigade, 6th of December, 1991, 1400 hours. Osojnik (Kupari)." If I may clarify. This document was written in Kupari and distributed in Osojnik, in my working notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Below that, we read: "Report on the combat activities of the 5th Battalion of the -- of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade, submitted to the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the reverse of that report, it says "Miroslav Jovanovic" -- rather, on the second page, it says "Miroslav Jovanovic," and there is a signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this report contain a description of the actions you undertook on the 6th of December and the operations executed by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under paragraph 2 of your report, it is mentioned that the idea presented by Captain Kovacevic on the way the combat operations were to be carried out was precise. What did this imply in terms of neighbours and support? In other words, neighbouring units and support.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That implied support targeting firing positions on the other side that could be jeopardising his units that were located in the zone of operations of the battalion under my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area of your observation post, as indicated in this report, is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This must be a local name for it. On the map, it is clear it is the central part of the range overlooking the Dubrovnik river, from which you can see the entire area clearly, whereas the place name I quoted here I heard from the local population and used it in the report. Rijeka Dubravacka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under paragraph 3 of your report, it says here that you were notified that an air raid alarm was sounded in Dubrovnik around 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My observation organs were in the immediate vicinity of Dubravacka Rijeka, so that they could see and hear directly what was going on and reported it to me. And I was able to see part of it from my observation post. After the general alarm was sounded, and assuming that the population had found cover in the shelters in the zone of operations of my unit, only that personnel remained that was engaged in immediate preparations for the upcoming operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to paragraph 3. There is a reference to a time period between 7.45 to 8.30 a.m., indicating that action according to a certain schedule had been taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This indication of where the targets were and the number of projectiles fired, is that part also accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noted at the end of paragraph 3 that this precise indication of time and location -- or rather, times and locations, were notified to the operations centre. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 of your report relates to this second request of fire support.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, you write in your report about precisely detected locations from which the enemy was firing.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sustain any losses yourself that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the front end, that is, on the line of blockade closer to Dubravacka Rijeka, Sergeant Trivundza was wounded in the head by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- or rather, were the men from your unit able to determine where the sniper was located?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the location?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The snipers fired continuously from the area Nuncijata, Sustjepan, which is the left bank of the Dubravacka Rijeka, or rather, the southern side, south of the Dubravacka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 6 of your report where it says: "After the termination of firing at 11.55, the request of Captain Kovacevic was still pending for support against the area of the Libertas Hotel." Can you tell me: What was it that you heard concerning this request for support by Captain Kovacevic, that is, from Captain Kovacevic, after 1200 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Kovacevic continued to insist on this support in the area of the Libertas Hotel, asking the use of weapons which have sufficient firing range, because he was still exposed to fierce fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the direction of that fire from the Libertas Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood from his request that this fire was targeting the area of Srdj, that is, his forces deployed partly in the area of Srdj, in a clearing, without any cover, and directly exposed to this fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he suffering losses that he mentioned in this request?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He mentioned a number of 17 men. He said 17 of his men had been killed. I later received precise information on his losses, after the battlefield was cleared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing about this report. The latter part of paragraph 6, according to which the order of warship Captain Milan Zec from the previous day stated that an absolute cease-fire was to take place as of 1200 hours. And it says: "I had consulted with the duty-officer of the operations centre of the 9th VPS, Lieutenant Colonel Kozaric, in relation to the pending actions. The named person transmitted the order to me that the cease-fire should be totally observed and that I was to report to the forward command post of the 9th VPS and write a report." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I kindly ask that this document be marked as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, could I ask whether you're near the end of your evidence from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think I could finish within ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, after writing this report at the forward command post of Kupari at 1400 hours, what did you do? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the forward command post of the VPS, I went to rejoin my unit at my command post in the area of Osojnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I continue, I forgot to ask you something else. If you can remember: Did anyone at all, around 10.00 a.m. on the 6th of December, 1991, prohibit you from opening fire? Were there any prohibitions discussed on that day around 10.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you returned to your battalion, did you receive any visits on the 6th of December, 1991? Did anyone call on you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: After 1800 hours - and I cannot remember the exact time - Colonel Gavro Kovacevic, assistant commander of the VPS for ground forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Gavro Kovacevic tell you anything during this inspection, during this tour?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All the commanders of subordinated units were present at my command post, and Gavro Kovacevic informed the entire staff present as follows, "Comrade Lieutenant Colonel, I am conveying to you the order of Admiral Jokic to the effect that you are hereby replaced, relieved of your duties, and you are required to leave the theatre of war as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this order, was anyone else mentioned, apart from Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I asked why Colonel Kovacevic only answered, "These are the orders. Once Vice Admiral Jokic returned from seeing the federal secretary Kadijevic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard that, did you contact anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to the commander of the 5th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He told me he knew about the order. He didn't know the reasons behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I of course note Your Honour's ruling before, but this does go outside, in my submission, the effect of the ruling in relation to the summaries provided. This wasn't in the summaries. My learned friend didn't make an application this morning to be allowed to present this particular piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, this does seem to be another new area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
