utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can confirm that with absolute certainty even without looking at my notes, namely, that I informed my colleagues that this order to replace the witness was something his own brigade was aware of. I am certain that I notified this orally for sure, and I'm now looking at the proofing notes, but I think I might have notified it in writing as well. So the order for him to be relieved of his duties was something that his brigade had already been aware of, meaning the 5th Brigade, that the witness was part of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you have in evidence now, Mr. Rodic, that the commander of the 5th Brigade knew about the order, he didn't know the reasons behind it. I think you should take that matter no further.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not going any further. I have just informed my learned friends thereof. Just a couple of more minutes, all in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you said that your brigade had been informed of your replacement without knowing the reasons. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 5th Brigade decided to send his assistant commander for morale to take over command over the battalion, while I should go back to the command of the 5th Brigade. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what really happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who replaced you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander of the 5th Brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Andrija Sljivic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He came to the command post on the 7th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the 7th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go through the procedure of transition of duty?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do afterwards? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: After handing over the command over the battalion, we went to the forward command post of the 9th VPS. We informed the command of the VPS of the completed transition of duty procedure, and I tried to contact Vice Admiral Jokic in order to find out why I had been replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone explain why you were replaced?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find Admiral Jokic in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Somebody from the command told me that he must be in Kumbor, and as the road towards Podgorica passes by Kumbor, I was going to stop by at Kumbor and find him there. However, in Kumbor, they didn't know where he was either, so I went on to Podgorica, reported to the brigade commander, and the brigade commander had no additional explanation to offer me except that the order was for me to be replaced and leave the theatre of war, return to Podgorica, and continue performing my establishment duties of Chief of Staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jovanovic: What effect did this have on your military career?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Officially, nobody cited any negative reason for my replacement, nor was it ever invoked in my later military career. However, this fact in itself finally sidelined me. I was moved from command responsibilities to operations responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your promotion in rank suffer for this reason?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until that happened, I was in the group of commanding officers with fast track promotions, and after that I moved to the regular track, so to speak, and my promotions came at three and a half to four-year intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, clearly, this is time for a break. Colonel Jovanovic, we are going to have a break now. I would suggest that you take the opportunity to freshen up, and we'll resume in 20 minutes' time. All right? Thank you. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it to be Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It is. I was just consulting Mr. Weiner about one very small point, Your Honour. If you could just bear with me for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Colonel Jovanovic, in a moment there will be some questions put to you on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Re. Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, can you see and hear me quite clearly in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, when Mr. Rodic cross-examined you -- or sorry, examined you, that you had kept a personal record or diary. What was this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The officer commanding the unit always keeps a notebook or a working document that he keeps right there. He receives tasks and he issues tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this your personal record of your daily tasks and orders and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a notebook which is officially signed for at the command's archive in the records, the official records. There is a degree of confidentiality that attaches to that notebook, and once the notebook is full, it is handed over to the officer in charge of the files, who then treats the notebook in keeping with the procedures that are in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your notebook in which you recorded your notes about what happened on the 5th and 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, at the beginning of 1992, the notebook was full. It was handed over to the officer in charge and a new notebook was taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep yourself copies of what was in that notebook, either a photocopy or a written record of what you had in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The most important things from the notebook are included in official reports anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- you've already told the Trial Chamber that what happened to you on the 6th of December was basically career-threatening. Did you not think to keep separate notes of the times and events, things that had happened, to assist you if needed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't understand my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No one ever accused me of anything, condemned me, and no one ever provided a single reason for my discharge, dismissal. The only explanation that was given was the one given by the commander of the 2nd Corps. Upon my return to Podgorica, he said, "We know that you are blameless, and you will not be held accountable for anything."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I'm actually asking you is whether you, for your own employment self-protection, made a note of what was in your official notebook or kept any separate personal notes in case you needed to refer to them in an employment-related capacity at any time.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time -- I withdraw that. I just want to confirm something from your evidence in chief, and that is that when you prepared your handwritten report - that's Exhibit D108 - you did so with the aid of this personal official notebook you just told us about, and it was from that notebook that you were able to record with accuracy these times and events?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying there will be nothing in the notebook which isn't in the report, D108? In other words, everything in the notebook that's relevant is in D108, your report?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you last see your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1992, when I handed it over to the officer in charge, who was in charge of receiving those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the situation is, as far as you are aware, as a former military officer, if we wanted to, we could approach the military -- the relevant military authorities in Belgrade and gain access to this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting they wouldn't have it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The grade of confidentiality for that particular notebook is confidential. According to regulations, that sort of document is only kept for a year. I may be wrong, but the time that it is kept for is certainly very limited. After that, it is destroyed. It is burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first contacted by Defence investigators or Defence lawyers to assist them in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: About a month and a half ago, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean late May?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who approached you, or who contacted you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I first received a phone call, and the next day I accepted, and a lawyer came to see me. His name was Vladimir Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell Mr. Petrovic about the report, D108, which is your report of the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did refer to that report, and I pointed out that it was precisely a document of that sort of nature that I could use to jog my memory as to the times and places involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Petrovic take a statement from you? That is, did he write something down and you signed it for him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he take notes while you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you meet with Mr. Petrovic for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in a house in the countryside. The atmosphere was relaxed, so I think it lasted for about one and a half, two, or even three hours. We just sat there and talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have at that meeting a copy of your report of the 6th of December that's Exhibit D108?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you next see it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to Mr. Petrovic in May, late May, did you tell him about the briefing on the 5th of December at Kupari, chaired by Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell him about the circumstances of your dismissal or removal from your post on the evening of the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell Mr. Petrovic what Admiral Jokic had said at that meeting on the 5th of December and what you had said to Admiral Jokic, that is, your conversation or exchange with Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well do you know Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I met him for the first time when the 3rd Battalion was re-subordinated to the command of the military naval sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That doesn't quite answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not too well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was as a result of Admiral Jokic's actions on the 6th of December that your career path changed and that you went from being in the fast track to command to the regular track to command. That's the way you see it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that sense, Admiral Jokic is to blame for your career setback, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic retired as early as May 1992. Therefore, he had no direct bearing later on, on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've never had a chance to speak to Admiral Jokic and ask him why he did this, have you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But even now you'd certainly like to, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to, very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because it's something that even all these years later, it's something that still concerns you or rankles you in a way, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't seem to find anyone who will give me a reason for those harsh words, "relieved of all duties."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You thought that what happened to you on the 6th of December was unfair, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if anyone was to be relieved of their command, it shouldn't have been you; it should have been someone else, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the action itself, what it was about or the consequences. My official superior, my official superiors, on several different occasions, emphasised that they knew I was blameless, and they told me I had nothing to worry about. In some way, this was some sort of compensation that I felt I received, compensation for having to leave the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it was -- you know it was unfair because you weren't in charge -- you weren't responsible for the shelling of the Old Town. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I must say I know nothing about the shelling of the Old Town or for the real reasons behind what happened, or the real reasons for my removal. Therefore, my removal has nothing to do with what was going on around the Old Town, in point of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened was that the Old Town was shelled on the 6th of December and someone was removed -- someone in a position of commanding mortars was removed, and that was you. Those are the facts, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us not twist these facts. The Old Town was not shelled by mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know the Old Town was shelled on the 6th of December, and you know that at the highest levels of the federal army there was great dissatisfaction about what had happened --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I don't know that, except that I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told that the Old Town was shelled; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that the Old Town was shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The men under my command certainly didn't fire on the Old Town. The information about the shelling is something that was received from the operations centre. Now, as for who shelled the town and when they shelled the town, and how, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying in all these years you haven't heard that Captain Kovacevic's unit was responsible for the shelling of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a story I heard in the public media, but, to be quite honest, I never found it necessary to look into what the real truth was. I only knew that it wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your knowledge of where artillery was stationed on the 6th of December, it could only have been artillery under Captain Kovacevic's command, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know, because I did not know the exact location of the firing positions or the target area that was being fired Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you feel that because you were the only person who was relieved of their command that day that you had been unfairly scapegoated for whatever had happened in Dubrovnik? Because you weren't the responsible person, it should have been someone else who was removed from their command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to jump to any conclusions as to why my removal occurred. I never came to my conclusions, nor do I have any particular conclusions now. As for my removal -- and again, I must go back to the statement that I gave attorney-at-law Rodic. I tried to get in touch with Admiral Jokic to find out what the reasons were for my removal. Not having tracked him down, the next day I got in touch with my superior command, the command of the 2nd Corps. The corps commander told me, literally, "We know that you are entirely blameless in connection with the Old Town or the shelling. You just carry on with your duties, because in the first place you were not the commander there. Therefore, you cannot be removed." Militarily speaking, this would be entirely justified and there would be an inherent logic to it. This was some sort of compensation for me as a soldier. It was enough for me to carry on with my duties, according to my establishment post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware, aren't you, that Captain Kovacevic was actually promoted shortly after the events of the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, because the command of the VPS and the 5th Brigade, or rather, the 2nd Corps, were separate units, and the 5th Brigade is within the 2nd Corps, and I am Chief of Staff of the 5th Brigade. Therefore, I was not receiving any official information from the VPS, only information in connection with my unit, with the 3rd Battalion, that sort of thing. I had no information on any other units in the VPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your report of the 6th of December with you in Belgrade or do we need to put it on the screen here for you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have the report in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to clarify something for me, if you could, and that is, if you look at the top, the first page, and the bottom of the second page, there is a stamp that says "military secret, confidential," photocopied, the date of 26th of December, 2003. Could you please give us some assistance in telling us why that stamp is there and what it means.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the heading of the report that I wrote in my own hand -- the rules of correspondence request that on the left-hand side you find what you find here. In the upper right-hand corner, you have the degree of confidentiality indicated, and as you see what I wrote here is "military secret, confidential." The document was based on a notebook that carries the same degree of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the notebook which you say would have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the document which was addressed in this way was sent to the command -- the battalion does not have its own stamp, this was sent to the command of the VPS, and the relevant body concluded that they should put a stamp on it. It is indeed their stamp; at least, in as far as I can see. This is a photocopy of an exemplar that was made on the 26th of December, 2003. And I assume that this is a document that was obtained from the archive of the VPS in December 2003. Photocopies were made and a stamp was put on it. The original copy still belongs to the VPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether that was done at the request of the Defence of General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea where this photocopy was obtained from. I just know that yesterday afternoon I was allowed to inspect this report. A month and a half ago, I emphasised the importance of this report, reckoning that it could be found, and I said I would like to have it, to look at it, so that I could refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you -- you wrote this report before you were aware that Admiral Jokic had ordered you removed from your -- relieved from your position, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware when you wrote this report that possible civilian targets -- possible civilian objects had been targeted or hit by JNA shelling during the course of the morning? You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your observation post, you couldn't see the Old Town, could you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you could see civilian areas of the broader area of Dubrovnik, couldn't you? The urban area of Dubrovnik surrounding the Old Town, around Babin Kuk and Lapad.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The northern reaches of Dubrovnik, which is what my observation post faced. I could see that part clearly, and I was in a position to clearly observe the firing points. And fire only on targets that were active, that were operating, that were firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That northern area of Dubrovnik of course includes -- is of course an urban area, isn't it, full of flats and houses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the entire area, which can be seen clearly from the observation post. Therefore, the firing positions where weapons were positioned were also clearly visible, the way they were deployed and whether or not they were firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your report doesn't say that you saw any soldiers in the streets of Dubrovnik, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to stress the following: My observation troops had informed, at 0700 hours, that a general alarm signal was sounded, that the population was taking shelter, and under the assumption that the people were going to their shelters, whereas those who were still on the move, who were going here and there in their vehicles, it was assumed that these people who were getting prepared for action. Now, whether they were located at Nuncijata or at Lazaret, it made no difference. These were people who were jeopardising our units. They are taking positions, preparing themselves, and opening fire. Therefore, at no time could we see civilians on the move, because between 7.00 and 7.35, when -- before we started actually opening fire from our positions, this was time enough for the population to take shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you wrote your report -- I withdraw that. You wrote your report after fire had been ordered to be ceased, didn't you, after you had received orders from above not to fire?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, you were aware of reports of civilians being killed in the Dubrovnik area by fire from the JNA, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware that parts of Dubrovnik had been damaged by JNA shelling, that's the greater area of Dubrovnik. You were aware of that at the time you wrote your report, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I had no information about the situation in the town. I was writing a report about my activities, about the fire that was opened, and the areas that were engaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the course of the morning, you, according to this report, had fired some 410 mortars. You were firing them, amongst other places, towards urban areas, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were firing in the areas where there were active targets, targets firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would expect, in firing 410 mortars in the course of a morning in areas that included urban areas, there would be civilian casualties, wouldn't you? When I said "mortars," I meant mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You must have misunderstood me. The general alert was sounded at 0700 hours, and the assumption was that the civilian population was in their shelters. Therefore, whoever was on the move, it was understood that this is -- these are people who are jeopardising our positions, who are firing at us, and as such constitute a threat to be fired upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not what your report says. Your report says you had concluded that the people who were moving around the town were the ones who were preparing for combat activities and were acting against the 3rd, 472nd. It doesn't say that you actually observed soldiers firing against your positions from Dubrovnik or that your soldiers or your men on the ground informed you that people were -- or soldiers were firing against your positions. It doesn't say that, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to point out that we fired only upon the firing positions that were active and opening fire, from my observation post and from the observation post of the lower levels of the battalion I commanded, one could clearly see the spot where there was a weapon opening fire from the areas of Sustjepan and Nuncijata. Those were the areas where the firing positions of the Croatian forces were, that were opening fire from their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if that's so, sir, there's absolutely no reason for you to put in the report anything about a conclusion about anyone who was on the streets after 7.00 a.m. must have been a soldier, was there? Because that would have been irrelevant for the purposes of your report if you were only firing upon fixed Croatian firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, sir. If you were only firing upon fixed Croatian military targets who were firing at you, there would be no reason for you to put in that report that anyone on the street after 7.00 a.m. must have been a soldier preparing for combat.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify one thing. Artillery does not open fire the way infantry weapon does, that you're visualising it, you're looking at a person and firing upon it. The fire support group, artillery fire support group, covers a certain area of deployment. Therefore, a fire support group opens fire at a certain area, not at a person. And the conclusion I draw here is exactly that, that I consider that the people have found shelter and that those who are on the move outside, if we still see them on the move, and that these are there to support the weapons. Because for the activity of artillery weapons, it is very important to detect the places where the projectiles are being fired from. And it is then on that particular area that one opens fire, and not on the people who are on the move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because, of course, people on the move could include those rushing to hospital or emergency services, police, fire, ambulance, medical workers, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't said this, nor have I actually seen people on the move, ambulances or anything of the sort you're suggesting. I was referring merely to the people on the move in the immediate area of the deployment of these weapons, the weapons that then immediately afterwards opened fire upon our forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your report says: "I had thus concluded that the citizens had hidden themselves in shelters and that the people who were moving around the town were the ones preparing for the combat activities." Your report does not confine the moving people to those in the immediate vicinity of a Croatian military target, such as a mortar, does it? It refers to all people walking around the town of Dubrovnik, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because it is not around Dubrovnik that I see these people on the move, but in the area where we spotted the activity of the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not what I'm asking you. Your report says "moving around the town." It says nothing about in the vicinity of military objectives or mortars, does it? Just please confine yourself to that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: People on the move. If you have a map in front of you, then you, for instance, see people on the move in the direction of Sustjepan. This is an area that is a clearing. You can clearly see people moving. You see people moving towards Nuncijata along certain points. And I suppose then that their intention is to prepare the combat weapons. And exactly that's why I put in my report that all the non-combatants were in shelter, and the detected fire targets clearly indicates that the people on the move are, in a way, in service of these weapons. Now, in this particular report, I did not put the exact location, nor the number of people on the move, and of course these are not many. These are only few people on the move. But I wish to stress again that weapons do not fire upon persons but upon the area in the immediate vicinity of the deployed weapon, in order to neutralise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your report, as written and as read to you just then, suggests that anyone in the open walking -- moving around the town after the air raid siren had sounded was a military objective. That's what it suggests, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It must suggest that --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The military target -- a military target, in my conclusion, constituted only the facility, the weapon, that was jeopardising my unit or the unit immediately adjacent to mine. Therefore, to make it clear: A military target, in my opinion, and this is not just my position; this is something that is as such, and I have to say that my troops were very well trained, capable, disciplined. They were not chaotic in their action. Rather, they were there to neutralise the detected military target that was active, and this was my opinion at the time and is still my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But even though you couldn't see or identify these people, that if anyone -- anyone on the street after 7.00 a.m., when the siren had sounded, was basically a target?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please -- can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're saying is that even if you couldn't see or identify these people who were on the streets after 7.00, your view was that if anyone was on the street after 7.00 moving around, they could be shot at?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the reason you have this in your report, I suggest, sir, is that you were aware when you wrote the report that there had been significant civilian casualties in Dubrovnik, and you had to find a way of explaining it. That is why you put in that anyone moving around the town after 7.00 was presumed to be connected with combat activities, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. You are presuming that you can say what it is that I think, and I could not know at the time that there were any civilians who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. victims. And now, so many years later, you are putting to me that I knew this at the time and that this was the reason why I put it in my report. Now, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to give you -- I'll give you a chance to tell us why you've put it in the report, because I don't think it's quite clear yet. Can you give us a logical explanation of why you would include something about people moving around the town of Dubrovnik if you didn't know there had been civilian casualties and you didn't know whether they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I detected persons moving in the area where the firing positions were, active firing positions, sources of fire. It is really far-fetched now to say that I knew of those civilian victims and this was the reason why I included it into my report. This might sound a bit illogical to you, but to this very day, I don't know how many or who the victims in Dubrovnik were. I knew of the activities, but I don't know these details. And this wasn't the reason why I wrote the report as it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hotel Libertas is, of course, in the middle of an urban area, isn't it, close to houses and flats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Hotel Libertas was not fired upon from mortars of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade, exactly because Captain Kovacevic conveyed his -- forwarded his request, and this is what I put in my report, because he had been under fire of the artillery pieces at Hotel Libertas, that he was then asking for weapons that would give him support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nuncijata and Luncijata, they're different places, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Luncijata, on the left bank of Dubravacka Rijeka, which is the northern slope of Srdj, closer to Dubravacka Rijeka, and to the east is Sustjepan. And this is the area I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that you didn't fire on Nuncijata, as opposed to Luncijata?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Luncijata.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fire on Nuncijata on the 6th of December, 1991, that is, your mortars?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the fire from the area of Luncijata and Sustjepan that was directly jeopardising the forces of the 3rd Battalion that I was in command of, and that is why our weapons opened fire on the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just -- to clarify that, can you just please tell the Trial Chamber where Nuncijata as opposed to Luncijata is.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have a map in front of me. If it's possible to have it on the screen. It should be further to the south or on the western slopes of Srdj. I can't really visualise it now in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness -- could P10 perhaps be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the map?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I would kindly ask the technician, if possible, to designate the area of Luncijata. I know where it is. Whereas for Nuncijata, I wouldn't be able to point that out, because it's impossible to see anything from where I'm sitting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just indicate the general area so we can move the map around to show you where Nuncijata is.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could put in the foreground Dubravacka Rijeka, and then I will find Luncijata, and perhaps then Nuncijata could be found by the very name that is written on the map. The map should be lowered further to see Dubravacka Rijeka, Sustjepan, and Luncijata. Yes, there it is. Let us see. You can see it's on the north-western slopes of Srdj, at Dubravacka Rijeka, Luncijata should be at the level of the number 38. Which one is it? Luncijata. And then to the east lies Sustjepan. And Nuncijata, I would ask you to point that out, because I can't really see it from here. Perhaps you can find it on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying you can't locate it on that map there, that is, the general area where Nuncijata should be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot locate Nuncijata, at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll move on from that particular point. Just on the issue of the Hotel Libertas, did Captain Kovacevic request that you fire upon the Hotel Libertas at about 10.15 to 10.20, because there were -- because his forces were being fired on from that location?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Kovacevic asked that fire be opened upon Lazaret, Libertas, after 9.00, because he detected fire being opened from there, and it was a threat to him. And then I forwarded his request to the operations centre, that he was requesting fire upon Libertas, and I opened fire at Lazaret because it was within my area of responsibility of my unit that Lazaret was situated, the northern part of Babin Kuk, whereas Libertas was outside the range of my weapons, and that's why I forwarded his request to the operations centre, with the probability that the 130-millimetre Howitzers would be able to fire at the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact fire some 27 shells at Libertas?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at Libertas. At 9.15, after having received his request, up until 11.55, the firing of these projectiles at the detected fire targets came -- was something that -- we were firing at those areas that were within our range, and Libertas was not within the range of the weapons of the artillery of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, I just want to show you an extract from the operations centre's war diary. That's D96.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could that please be placed on the ELMO. That's the page between 66 and 67.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you may have a copy of it there with you in Belgrade. I think the registrar was taking one with her.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the page between 66 and 67.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, do you have it in front of you? That's the page between 66 and 67.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just read the entry. It says: "Overview of events, 6/12/91." I think it would be the fourth paragraph. It says: "At the request of Kovacevic." Just read on from what it says. Read aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "At the request of Kovacevic, the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade, between 10.15 and 10.20, fired three platoons of 120 millimetres (27 shells) on Libertas."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "Two times six of 120 millimetres (12 shells)." Full stop. They were hit by the firing position of the enemy of 82-millimetre mortars. I can explain this in the following way: In the reports that I regularly sent through means of communication - I or my observer - covers the contents of Mr. Kovacevic's request, requiring fire to be opened on Libertas. He required fire on Libertas, whereas the fire actually opened was within the firing range of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade, not including Libertas. You will find somewhere in that war diary that Kovacevic wrote this request, requiring fire to be opened on Libertas. It is possible that the person who made this entry noted this fact in this form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what it suggests, just the way it's written, is that your brigade fired first of all 27 shells and then 12 shells at -- successfully at Libertas at Captain Kovacevic's request. That's what it says, doesn't it? When I said "brigade," I meant battalion.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Battalion, yes. Yes. But this reference to Libertas is not due to the fact that Libertas was a target. What it says here, that targets were detected sources of fire. That is the essence, not that Libertas was a target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It actually seems to say that you hit Libertas. It says that, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Successfully fire was opened against firing positions." It is nowhere written that Libertas had been hit, especially because 120-millimetre weapons did not have the required range and did not even attempt to target Libertas. I don't see where you find this conclusion that Libertas was successfully hit. I made my comment on what is written here, because it was I personally who forwarded Kovacevic's request requiring fire support, among other things, against Libertas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, sir, that's consistent with what is written in the war diary, I suggest is consistent with what is written in paragraph 4 of your report of the 6th of December. If you could just turn to that. Which says: "Around 9.00 I had once again received a request from Captain Kovacevic to continue with the support and acted on the regions on the of Velika Petka, Babin Kuk, Hotel Libertas, as well as on the regions where fire targets and fire positions had been located, along with the MB targets of the enemy. I had informed the operative centre of the 9th VPS of the contents of the request, as well as with the action taken with recourse of the 3rd, 5th Partisan Motorised Brigade." Do you follow? What I'm suggesting, when you read the two together, sir, we've got you saying in your report, "I was requested to fire on the Libertas and I reported back on the action taken with that recourse." And then the war diary, or the operations centre war diary suggests that that is in fact what you did, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the quintessential things that I'm emphasising. In the request of Kovacevic, the area of Libertas is included. The area of Libertas, as the command of the VPS knows and as Kovacevic probably also knows as well, is beyond my firing range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told him that, didn't you? I withdraw that. I assume you told him that, that it was beyond your firing range. You would have told him as early as 9.00 when he asked for that support, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he understood that, I assume, after you told him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are turning things upside down a bit here. Kovacevic is requesting support. I forward his request to the superior command, to the operations sector, and I do open fire within the area covered by my battalion. But I also forward that part of his request where he's requesting fire on Libertas. He is requesting specifically 130-millimetre Howitzers. I do what I can with my abilities, and I inform the operations centre between 9.10 and 11.50 that I am acting with my weapons and I am implementing Kovacevic's request. I also notify the operations centre thereof. This entry, formulated in this way, can be originating from the contents of the request written by Kovacevic rather than a list of actions undertaken by the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify this. Are you saying you personally informed the operations centre that your mortars were -- that Libertas was outside the range of your mortars and they would have to get support from somewhere else? Is that what you informed them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give them orders. I just forwarded Kovacevic's request, emphasising that I am providing request, firing on the targets within my zone of responsibility: Babin Kuk, Sustjepan, and Lazaret. Therefore, I'm reporting on the scope of my activities. I am not giving them tasks to provide support from somewhere else. They command the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying. I'm asking you -- I withdraw that. You're saying Kovacevic told you he wanted support from Libertas which was firing on him. He told the operations centre -- did you tell the operations centre that you, your unit, could not provide that support because it was outside of range? Because I suggest it would have been a very important thing to tell them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Plus I emphasised --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That should be recorded --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this for the fifth time. I emphasised that I personally notified the operations centre that this can be done by 130-millimetre weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that your notification to the operations centre passing on that important pieces of information, that is, that the Libertas which was firing upon Kovacevic's forces was outside of range, outside of your range, that could be hit by -- was within the range of 130-millimetre weapons, should be recorded in the operations centre diary.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was my assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you assessed it, it should have been recorded in the operations diary, there would be no reason for Kovacevic to continue -- please let me finish. There would be no reason for Kovacevic to continue asking you for support to hit the Libertas if you had in fact passed on that extremely important communication, would there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are again suggesting an answer that does not exist. It is not within my competence to issue orders. I cannot suggest that Howitzers be used. They're under the command of the VPS. It is purely my assessment on the battlefield. I am saying that only these weapons can do the job. As far as Kovacevic's tasks are concerned, he is requesting support against the sources of fire which endanger him, and I suppose he also addressed the command of the VPS. And if communications allowed it, he spoke with the crews of the Howitzers themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to draw your attention that I believe my learned friend, Mr. Re, is not phrasing his questions in such a way as to present to the witness accurately the contents of the war diary before him. In fact, he is making assertions contrary to those in this war diary, and he's misleading the witness by misrepresenting the contents. I would like my learned friend to pay attention to the entry made at 9.50 of the 6th December, because this is all this witness is speaking to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you've heard that. I leave you to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, sir, what -- after you told the operations centre that 130-millimetre action or support was required, there would be no reason Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for Kovacevic, some two hours later, still to be requesting support from you against Libertas, would there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Please, I would appreciate it very much to ask the Trial Chamber to ask the Prosecutor to study a little the regulation of the army and the rules of command and control. I was in the role of battalion commander, and my sole competence was to command and to control the fire opened by my immediate subordinates. As far as reports and requests are concerned, subordinated commanders direct them directly to the command of the VPS. It is not my job to direct, plan, and target the action of all subordinated units of the VPS. I don't know what the Prosecutor is making, whether he is trying to insinuate something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to your report, at paragraph 6, it says: "After the actions have ceased, at 11.55, there still existed a request on the part of Captain Kovacevic to provide support against the region of the Hotel Libertas." What I'm suggesting to you, as a military officer in command of that particular battalion on that day, your having informed the operations centre that you could not provide that support, only 130-millimetre weapons could, there would be no reason for Kovacevic to persist with his request for support from you, would there? That is some two hours after you've informed the operations centre of this major problem.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, when you insist on such questions, I in turn insist on my answer. It is all about the VPS. It's in their competence to decide the request of Kovacevic, which I only forwarded. Second, why don't you ask yourself the question: What a battalion commander is supposed to do if I am informed by a cooperating commander that he is suffering great losses, he has a lot of people wounded, he cannot pull out, and he's still under fire from Libertas Hotel? What happened, we find out around 1700 hours that a lot of people were wounded and killed at Srdj. 17 men were killed at Srdj, more precisely. What do I do next? I request -- in fact, he requests support against Libertas because that's the area that's endangering him. You should ask the question of the command of the VPS, how they responded to this request and what they actually did. I am telling you of what I did that was within my authority in response to his request. I organised fire against the named targets in the zone of responsibility of my units. At 11.50, I reported on my progress, and you see in item 6 of that report what was done after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what time are we going to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Hopefully to finish the witness, which I assume you will be doing reasonable shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Reasonably shortly. There are some matters I need to put to him. I'm just wondering about tapes and times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've still got some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the way paragraph 6 reads, and I suggest the only possible way you can read it, is that you're saying as of 11.55, that's five minutes before the cease-fire was supposed to come into operation, there was an outstanding request to you of -- from Kovacevic for support against the Hotel Libertas area. But because the cease-fire was going -- was about to take place, you were concerned to act upon it. Therefore, you consulted with Colonel Kozaric in relation to it, and that is why you didn't give support in relation to the Hotel Libertas. I suggest, sir, if you read it, that is the only way you can read what you have written there, that is, Kovacevic wanted you to fire on the Libertas, but because it was five minutes to 12.00, you checked, and didn't.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You asked the question whether a Howitzer 130-millimetre fire was opened. From this entry, you can conclude that it wasn't. I am asserting: If I had been able to fire against detected targets with my own weapons, their weapons would certainly have been neutralised, considering that their combat units were still firing. I asked whether to continue with my activities, because in the zone of responsibility of my unit, enemy action was still going on. Libertas was pointed as a key facility because fire from that facility was putting us in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, can you suggest why Kovacevic would be requesting fire from you, still at 11.55, if he should have been aware at that point that you couldn't provide that support? Is there any reason you can give for that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do have a reason. You can ask a psychologist how a man feels when he sees 15 to 20 men lying dead within 50 metres of him, and everyone in that position starts clutching at straws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about this briefing you say you went to on the 5th of December, 1991. Where exactly was this briefing, exactly, the exact location? You said it was in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Briefings took place in Kupari, and there was a room used by the operations centre, the forward command post of the VPS, the naval sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was in the room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furniture? Maps? Radios? What was in the room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: A soldier needs only say that it was an organised operations centre of the naval sector from which the subordinated units of the naval sector were being commanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're before an International Criminal Tribunal at the moment, and I want to know what was in the room.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Certain means of communication, maps, desks and chairs, a conference table perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, "perhaps"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Facilities for holding meetings of the operations centre of the naval sector. Tables and chairs we used to sit when we attended these briefings and the means of communications that were installed so that we could maintain communication with subordinated units and so that commanders of certain units within the sector could continue performing their tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Are you saying that it was conducted around a table, in a room containing communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are twisting things again. Means of communication are located in one part of the room. They serve to maintain communications for control and command, whereas another part of the room is adapted for holding conferences, for holding meetings of the operations centre. This larger area is equipped for holding the meetings and performing the task of commanding and controlling units from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Where did the briefing on the 5th of December take place? Which part of this -- which part of this briefing area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the operations centre of the 9th Naval Sector, at the command post, or rather, the forward command post of the 9th Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you seem to be having some difficulty in describing the room in which the briefing took place. I want you to tell us about the room. What was in the room where you were and where all the other people were during the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I attended my first briefing on the 5th. That was the first time I was there. Second, I came in the role of the commander of the 3rd Battalion to attend the briefing. I was interested in the commander of the VPS, so that I can inform him of the activities of my unit and receive tasks for the next day. The point of that briefing is that we meet there. The commander sits in his place. The other commanders sit behind the table around him, according to position, and the briefing goes on. I don't know what kind of detail you want me to describe. This is the essential description of that room, equipped for work. The commander has the central place --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a round table, a square table, rectangular table, a series of tables, benches, chairs? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know, to tell you the truth. Listen, I spent ten years serving as Chief of Staff. When you ask me now what my desk looked like, my own desk and the conference table I used myself, I would find it difficult to answer. And I spent ten years in that office. That facility was normally used as some sort of hotel, and it was only adapted for the purposes of the operations centre. I did see it. I was there. But I really cannot remember it in detail now when you ask the question this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Admiral Jokic seated in relation to the other people at this briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was seated at the head of that room where the officers were seated because he was the one who chaired the meeting. Next to him there was Chief of Staff Milan Zec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was there? I want you to name the other participants in this briefing by name, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one thing you should bear in mind is that, in my official capacity as commander of my unit, I was within the 2nd Corps and not within the VPS. Therefore, as concerns the names, the only names I was familiar with were that of Vice Admiral Jokic, that of warship Captain Milan Zec, Lieutenant Colonel Kozaric. He was the operations officer that I was in touch with. We exchanged information. The assistant for moral guidance, Lieutenant Colonel Zarkovic, if I remember correctly. That particular evening, I can't specifically remember if the assistant for land forces, Colonel Gavro Kovacevic was there or not. These were the people I knew personally, as well as their names. As for the remaining officers, navy officers who were there, I really didn't deem it necessary for me to know their names and know them personally. I heard what they had to say, their contributions to the briefing, which concerned me very little, truth to tell, and that's all I needed to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only briefing you ever attended there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That morning I had taken up my duty as battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very same day, the 5th of December. Well, what time did this briefing commence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The usual practice was past 1800 hours, but the exact time depended on when all those officers who were supposed to attend came in, So that depended. As for that particular evening, I'm not sure what time it was, but it was half 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just repeat the last part of your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was after 1800 hours, because that evening I had left my command post at about 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the meeting go for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting went on for about one or one and a half hours, because I was back at my command post at about 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether notes were kept or minute -- notes or record was made of this meeting? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The operations duty-officer would have been duty-bound to keep minutes, but that's the VPS command, and I had no power over that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that meeting, it would have been apparent that your unit or battalion was the only one which could provide the necessary fire support to the JNA against Croat positions in Babin Kuk and Lapad, et cetera, if they were to assault Srdj the next morning; correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Part of Babin Kuk, the north-facing slope, yes. As for the section facing south, I was in no position to fire at that portion. That would have been the last ultimate line where the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade could provide any support at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, I just -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the signals and the time. There are some more areas I wish to cover. I realise I can't complete it in the time available today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination at this point, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of all the circumstances, as well as those of a more technical nature, I will only have three or four questions left for my re-examination. I will do my best to keep it as brief as possible. There are two or three things that need clarifying, something specific and something from the diary that I wish to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The length of the tape and the capacity of the supporting staff to keep going is the problem at the moment. We have the videolink at the moment. The present tapes have nearly run out. What the Chamber will do, Mr. Re, is adjourn now for 20 minutes, resume. You can have ten more minutes, and Mr. Rodic will have five minutes. And I hope that the support staff will understand that and we can then break for the day with the videolink completed. So we will resume at 25 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I see the witness is back in his place. Thank you for that, Mr. Jovanovic. Now, Mr. Re, if you'd like to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I just want to take you back to your report, which is D108. Now, in this report, you didn't mention Admiral Jokic by name. This is the report you made on the 6th of December, 1991. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never said in that report that Admiral Jokic was at that meeting, that briefing, on the 5th of December. You didn't say that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say in the report what the briefing on the 5th was about. The report contains reference to activities that took place on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never said you went to a meeting the day before, chaired by Admiral Jokic, did you, in that report?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The report is not supposed to contain any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never said you spoke to Jokic at that meeting. That's not in your report either, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I would like to say the following: The substance of this report is about the scope of activities that took place on the 6th of December. This is a combat report from a front. This is not a report of a briefing. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There would be no reason to refer to a briefing or a presentation by Captain Kovacevic the previous day if that's correct, would there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because if what you're saying in Court today is true, you could only be referring to the briefing by Kovacevic in paragraph 2, couldn't you? You just told us there would be no reason to refer to it because it's not that sort of report.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Only what was related to the activities. Please keep that in mind. Paragraph 2 is worded in such a way precisely for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic's presence at the meeting, his speaking to you, your questions to him, et cetera, is unrelated to these activities, nothing to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Activities that took place on the 6th are contained in the report. There is only a remark in paragraph 2, an analogy to the plan put forward by Kovacevic to the effect that the activities around Srdj had been postponed. In my reasoning, it wasn't necessary to go into any further details from the previous briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not a remark, sir; it's a justification for what occurred, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If an activity is planned and carried out, then there must be a reason, which is the continuity of life and work on the front. And now what you're asking me to do is, within that ongoing continuity, to pre-date the activities that took place on the 6th as having occurred on the 5th. I am only referring to those that occurred on the 5th. For example, I don't state anywhere in my report that a handover had taken place with the battalion commander. Whatever happened on that day is included in the report. This is, after all, a combat report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 is simply a justification for your own activities, your own actions, on the 6th of December, isn't it? Your reference to what Kovacevic did the day before is merely a justification for what you did on the 6th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not a justification. It's an explanation of how things happened, of how the activities were carried out that had been planned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Mr. Jovanovic, did you tell Mr. Petrovic that you had certain fears concerning the allegations -- one of the allegations in the indictment, that is, you were concerned that you yourself might be in danger of prosecution or indictment yourself if you were to come to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're telling us you've got no fear of coming to The Hague to give evidence, because you think you did nothing wrong on the day, and the civilian casualties had nothing to do with you, so you have nothing to fear?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have nothing to fear. There is no reason for me to have anything to fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the -- I'd like you to turn again to the war diary, which is D96. You've got a copy there with you. And if you could please turn to page 70, that's 7-0. I want to take you to a particular entry at 1500 hours. And it says -- it's a remark by Captain Barakovic: "The 3/5 Partisan Motorised Brigade is sustaining strong sniper fire from Sustjepan. One senior officer wounded and two vehicles were damaged. They were ordered to take the men to cover. Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic has ordered the same. He is ordering that 120-millimetre mortar brigade fire is to fire on the military targets with the purpose of protecting the people." That suggests that you were still firing at 3.00 p.m. that afternoon, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: 1500 hours. I was on my way from Kupari to Osojnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about two entries in this and then we'll finish. That's the first entry. What I'm saying to you is it suggests that you were firing or ordering the firing on military targets, it says, in the Sustjepan area as late as 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that what happened, you were still firing at 3.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At 1500 hours, Barakovic, an active duty-officer from that unit, reported that from Sustjepan there was sniper fire putting at risk the men of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just rereading it --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Is it correct that you were firing as late as 3.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, this is a war logbook of the navy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you firing as late as 3.00 p.m. or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: After arriving at the observation post -- no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next entry --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At 1500 hours, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next entry is at page 72, the time 1627. I'll just read it to you while you're finding it: "The 3/5 Partisan Motorised Brigade from 1545 to 1615 has acted with MB 120-millimetre fire on Sustjepan from which it has suffered strong and focused sniper fire. 1615 hours, stopped the action, 3 to 3/5 and 4 to 3" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apologise. "Against Kolocep during the day." This says that your battalion was still firing at Sustjepan between 1545 and 1615, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: 1615 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that in fact what you were doing, still firing as late as 1615 that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is of course some two hours -- more than two hours after you wrote this handwritten report which is D108? And --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understand. Which exhibit are you referring to? Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your report of the 6th of December. Two hours after you wrote that, you're still firing.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Brief explanation, please. At 1500 hours, I am at the forward command post of the VPS. Captain Barakovic is reporting about intense sniper fire. I give orders to carry out preparations and not to fire before my arrival until I came to assess the situation. Having arrived at the observation post, I noticed that there was sniper fire from the Sustjepan area, and I ordered the mortars to start firing at the area where sniper positions had been observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have nothing else, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, we don't have much time, so I will only ask you very few questions, and please, can you focus your attention on document D96, which is the war log, that I assume you have in front of you. Can you please look at page 68 of the war log, the entry at 0855.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything specified there as to the targets and the missiles that your units used up while firing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the remark there, in my report, it says "Luncijata," and in the war log it says "Nuncijata," the Nuncijata area. But it was wasn't the area that I was firing at. It was the Luncijata area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if both these locations actually exist, Luncijata and Nuncijata?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of their existence, because I've heard the name Nuncijata used during briefings. But the Luncijata area was within the area of responsibility of my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please first of all describe when you say Luncijata, with an L, as in London, where is this precisely?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did ask for a map on the ELMO. That was on the slopes of Srdj, facing north-west. I can't tell you the exact location now, because I don't have a map, but that's the Srdj slope facing north-west. And from there, from Luncijata, once you leave the port of Gruz and head east along Rijeka Dubrovacka, first you cross Luncijata and then you come to a sign saying "Sustjepan."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please try not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please display the map that has been marked as P11 now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at the map marked P11 and at the location called Gruz. In relation to this location, can you describe where the area was where you said you were opening fire from.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have the map and we don't see it either on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until you get the map on the screen, I would kindly ask you to compare this specific information as to the number of projectiles fired with point 3 of your report, whether they tally in quantities and in the spots they were fired from, in the positions they were fired from.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The specification, does it tally with the specification contained in the summary of events contained between pages 66 and 67 of the war log of the operations centre of the forward command post at Kupari? Does this particular specification also tally with your report?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my report - that is, the items listed in my report - do tally with the war log in terms of the quantity of projectiles, except for the location of the firing position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in terms of it being named as Luncijata or Nuncijata?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
